_strings.@@a606f17ea3fe: Treaty conformity — NE conforms to federal treaty treatment — income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is also excluded from NE income (it flows through the federal starting point; do not add it back on the NE return). (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state can conform on treaties while DECOUPLING from the federal Code for deductions or credits; see any law-change lines below.) State note: Nebraska's resident return (Form 1040N) starts from federal adjusted gross income: 2025 line 5 is "Federal adjusted gross income (AGI) (line 11a, Federal Form 1040 or 1040-SR) Do not leave blank." Federally treaty-exempt income is already excluded from federal AGI and therefore flows through. The only additions to federal AGI are on Nebraska Schedule I, Part A ("Adjustments Increasing Federal AGI"), whose 2025 line items are: (1) interest income from state/local obligations exempt from federal tax, (2) exempt interest from Nebraska obligations, (3) total taxable interest (line 1 minus line 2), (4) Financial Institution Tax Credit claimed, (5) Nebraska College Savings Program recapture, (6) Nebraska Enable plan recapture, (7) federal net operating loss deduction, (8) S corporation or LLC Non-Nebraska loss, (9) Nebraska PTET deducted under IRC section 164, (10) Relocation Incentive Act employee recapture, (11) loss on the sale or exchange of gold or silver bullion included in federal AGI, and (12) Food Bank/Food Pantry/Food Rescue donation amounts deducted as a federal charitable contribution. NONE of these requires adding back income exempt under a U.S. income tax treaty. With no treaty add-back and a federal-AGI starting point, treaty-exempt income is not re-taxed -> Nebraska conforms.

Nebraska's convenience-of-the-employer rule as AMENDED by LB 1023 for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025: where a nonresident is paid for services performed outside Nebraska that are directly related to a business, trade, or profession carried on within Nebraska and, except for the nonresident's convenience, could have been performed in Nebraska — "Only the compensation paid for services performed within Nebraska constitutes Nebraska sourced income of the nonresident under this provision." Trigger: A nonresident working remotely for a Nebraska business, trade, or profession (the pre-2025 rule sourced convenience-based out-of-state wages TO Nebraska; the TY2025 amendment narrows Nebraska-source income to Nebraska-performed services). [Nebraska Department of Revenue, "2024 Nebraska Legislative Changes" — LB 1023 nonresident compensation sourcing, effective for taxable years beginning on or after 2025-01-01. — https://revenue.nebraska.gov/about/2024-nebraska-legislative-changes] If the rule reaches these wages, a NONRESIDENT NE return is required that the physical footprint alone never shows.

Adjudication note (two-pass): vector exemption counts are zero by design — Nebraska personal exemptions are a $171-per-person nonrefundable CREDIT on Form 1040N line 18 for 2025 (raised from $166 in 2024 and $157 in 2023), never an income exemption, so the pack ships no personal/dependent keys and the engine refuses nonzero counts. Nebraska personal exemptions are a TAX CREDIT, not an income exemption: Form 1040N line 18 gives RESIDENTS a nonrefundable credit of $171 times the number of Nebraska personal exemptions on line 4 (yourself, spouse, and dependents; the 2025 form prints '$171 times the number on line 4'). It is subtracted from tax, not from income, so no personal/dependent amounts are shipped in exemptions; calc.state_tax applies it past the tax line when exemption_credit_counts is passed (tax.exemption_credits, Phase K JK28) (nonresidents and partial-year residents claim it prorated on Nebraska Schedule III, line 7). The shipped standard deduction is the 2025 chart amount with ZERO boxes checked on Form 1040N line 2a (under 65, not blind) for a filer who cannot be claimed by another taxpayer for the federal child tax credit or dependent tax credit. Nebraska Standard Deduction Chart with line-2a boxes checked: Single $10,600 (1 box) / $12,600 (2); Married Filing Jointly $18,850 / $20,500 / $22,150 / $23,800 (1-4 boxes); Qualifying surviving spouse $18,850 / $20,500 (1-2); Married Filing Separately $10,250 / $11,900 / $13,550 / $15,200 (1-4; the spouse's 65-and-over and blind boxes count only if the primary taxpayer can claim a personal exemption for the spouse); Head of Household $14,600 / $16,600 (1-2). These are NOT applied by calc.state_tax — use the chart amount on line 6. If you or your spouse CAN be claimed by another taxpayer for federal child tax credit or dependent tax credit purposes, your standard deduction is the SMALLER of the federal standard deduction allowed on line 12e of Federal Form 1040/1040-SR or the Nebraska chart amount — not modeled; compute on the form. Itemizers are not modeled: taxpayers who itemized on the federal return take the LARGER of the Nebraska standard deduction (line 6) or Nebraska itemized deductions (line 9 = federal Schedule A line 17 total minus line 8, the state and local income taxes reported on federal Schedule A line 5a — which must be entered even if the total state and local taxes were limited to $40,000, or $20,000 married filing separately, on federal Schedule A line 5e). If you used the federal standard deduction you MUST use the Nebraska standard deduction (booklet, Line 6). Nebraska Schedule I adjustments (Form 1040N line 12 adjustments increasing federal AGI from Schedule I line 13, line 13 adjustments decreasing federal AGI from Schedule I line 44) are NOT modeled — if they apply, fold them into the supplied base per the base guidance or compute line 14 on the form. New Schedule I Part A lines for 2025 include the Relocation Incentive Act employee recapture, losses on the sale or exchange of gold or silver bullion, and the addback of food-donation amounts deducted federally. Tax table option (paper filers only): 'Only taxpayers filing paper returns may use the Nebraska Tax Table'; electronic filers must use the Tax Calculation Schedule (booklet, Line 15), which is the exact bracket math this op implements. The table calculates tax at the midpoint of each $100 band and covers Nebraska taxable income up to $77,760 (2024: $75,360), so a paper filer's table amount may differ by a few dollars from this op's result within a band; above $77,760 the booklet worksheet is (taxable income - $77,760) x .0520 plus $3,566 Single/MFS, $3,088 MFJ/QSS, or $3,276 HoH — each of which is the shipped schedule evaluated at $77,760 and rounded to whole dollars. Qualifying surviving spouse: the schedule's second table is titled 'Married Taxpayers, Filing Jointly and Qualifying Surviving Spouses' — the engine's QSS-to-MFJ mapping is exact for the brackets, and the QSS standard deduction with zero boxes is the same $17,200. Married filing separately is printed with the SAME schedule as Single on the 2025 Tax Calculation Schedule (identical breakpoints $4,030/$24,120/$38,870 and identical constants $99.14/$804.30/$1,543.28) — copied from the MFS table, not derived by halving MFJ. Nonresidents and partial-year residents are NOT modeled: they compute line 15 via Nebraska Schedule III (line 9), which apportions the tax by the Nebraska-income ratio from Schedule III line 4.
